title: Support vector machines
summary: Find a separating hyperplane with a large margin, optionally in an implicit feature space.
why: Controls decision-boundary complexity through margin and regularization.
interview: Derive the margin, dual constraints, and kernel validity.
derivation: The canonical planes w.x+b=+1 and -1 are each 1/||w|| from the decision plane, giving width 2/||w||. This uses the canonical scaling of w and b.

KKT conditions include primal feasibility, dual feasibility, stationarity, and complementary slackness. A valid kernel produces positive semidefinite Gram matrices; Mercer conditions provide a classic characterization under regularity assumptions.

steps.note: RBF distance is highly sensitive to feature scale.
Kernel training can become expensive at large N.
Sign gives class; probabilities need separate calibration.

traps: Larger C penalizes slack more strongly and may overfit.
Large gamma creates very local RBF influence.
Kernel similarity scores are not calibrated probabilities.
tradeoff: Linear solvers scale well on sparse high-dimensional data; nonlinear kernels can require many support-vector comparisons.

explanations.title: Canonical margin and soft-margin slack
paragraphs: A linear classifier uses sign(w dot x + b). Under canonical scaling, margin planes are w dot x+b=+1 and -1. Distance to a plane divides the score by ||w||, so the full margin width is 2/||w||.

Minimizing half the squared norm maximizes this margin subject to correct separation. Soft-margin SVM adds nonnegative slack and a C penalty so noisy or overlapping data can violate the margin. Larger C penalizes violations more strongly.

A point can be correctly classified while lying inside the margin. Margin violation and classification error are therefore different. Feature scaling changes the geometry of the margin, making a train-fitted scaler part of an SVM pipeline.

explanations.title: The dual, support vectors, and KKT conditions
paragraphs: Introduce multipliers alpha_i for margin constraints. Stationarity gives w=sum alpha_i*y_i*x_i and sum alpha_i*y_i=0, with 0<=alpha_i<=C. The dual depends on pairwise dot products, which permits a kernel substitution.

KKT includes primal feasibility, dual feasibility, stationarity, and complementary slackness. Points with alpha=0 do not contribute to the decision function. With 0<alpha<C, a point lies on the margin under the standard soft-margin solution; alpha=C can indicate a margin violation.

The prediction is a weighted sum over support-vector kernel evaluations plus b. The number of support vectors directly affects nonlinear SVM inference cost. A linear model can collapse that sum into one weight vector.

explanations.title: Linear, polynomial, and RBF kernel behavior
paragraphs: A kernel computes an inner product in an implicit feature space. For finite sample sets its Gram matrix should be positive semidefinite; classic Mercer conditions provide a characterization under regularity assumptions. An arbitrary similarity is not automatically a valid kernel.

Linear kernels use x dot xprime. Polynomial kernels use (gamma*x dot xprime+coef0)^degree. RBF uses exp(-gamma*||x-xprime||^2). Large gamma gives narrow influence and potentially complex boundaries; small gamma gives broader influence. Tune gamma together with C.

For large datasets, storing and optimizing a dense kernel matrix can be prohibitive. Compare a linear SVM or approximate features. SVM decision scores are not calibrated probabilities by default; probability calibration needs separate validation.
